full_text:
Interviewer:	Okay how are you getting on, on placement then?

Subject:	It's all right actually, it's all right yeah erm (inaudible) yet. (Good) It didn’t take me long to settle in probably about a couple of days to be honest yeah so.

Interviewer:	That's good.

Subject:	No it's all right.

Interviewer:	Good when did you start then?

Subject:	12th of July.

Interviewer:	In the summer?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	So it's been quite a while now then?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	So can you tell me a bit about the organisation that you're working for then?

Subject:	I work for [company] erm which is a textiles company as part of the (inaudible) the company make textiles, well just man-made acrylics and stuff and so like carbon fibre because carbon fibre goes into making erm like plane wings and stuff and then there's like right through to textiles that just make you know clothes. So that's, that…

Interviewer:	Quite diverse then? 

Subject:	Yeah and we just make specialities which are you know the, hard to make wearables whatever but we’re not selling very many of them.

Interviewer:	OK how would you describe the company’s attitude to women?

Subject:	Hmm hmm, erm they're not really bothered actually I mean because I'm young it's a bit there a bit, some of the blokes are a bit you know about me and my thoughts and stuff but now it's all right you know. It probably took about 3 or 4 months for them to get used to me being there which is weird really because the student last year was a female so I didn’t think it would be a problem. But then I don’t from my approach it didn’t really she just kind of did her own thing a lot whereas I go out and you know chat to people and.

Interviewer:	Yeah so you're quite different people?

Subject:	Yeah, yeah.

Interviewer:	Okay how useful do you think that your degree so far has been to the work that you're doing there.

Subject:	Very useful.

Interviewer:	You are actually using stuff then?

Subject:	Yeah, yeah erm I mean some stuff if I didn’t have a degree I think I’d be all right like Health and Safety stuff I think it's just a lot of common sense but at the same time you do need to have that on board. You need to know about process engineering to appreciate it I mean we did I mean we have had some modules on safety and whatever and they’ve been very useful. I mean some of the stuff that I've done so far (inaudible) but some of the modules I haven’t used at all. You don’t really need them because you know there's computer programmes that do it for you do you see what I mean? (Yeah) Like we’ll just you know get, get your get all I mean obviously you need them so you know what data to get but once you’ve got that you don’t really need to actually know what you're doing.

Interviewer:	OK so do you feel that there's other things that you might have been better off learning at university instead then?

Subject:	Yeah, I mean well I've slightly changed my course so I’m doing environment protection which I wasn’t doing before and you do need to know a lot of environmental stuff I find. I mean I don’t know what it's like for other people.

Interviewer:	How did you decide to change your course then?

Subject:	 (Inaudible)

Interviewer:	If it's what you want to do.

Subject:	Yeah I mean like erm Health and Safety laws and stuff are changing all of the time and there's so many of them now that are changing like every 3 or 4 years that you just and they cost the company a lot of money to keep changing? (Yeah) Erm and I just think there'll be more jobs in that in the future because there's more and more of them you know. Like everyone sues everyone now so you need to be you know at that standard otherwise you're just going to get you know.

Interviewer:	Did you decide to do that after you had started on placement then?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the university could do more to prepare you for the placement?

Subject:	I was all right actually but I don’t know about, I don’t know about other people. I'm just kind of taking it as it comes so (if they hadn’t said anything to me I think I'd have been fine?)

Interviewer:	Yeah okay before you started placement did the uni or your department tell you what they expected you to get from the placement?

Subject:	Well like they email you like a bit of paper just sort of saying what you must and mustn’t do but not really it's just you just get the experience yourself. I mean I'm quite lucky with where I am because I've got loads of different projects but if I you know want to work more on one particular project then that would be seen and I would get more products that are like that but no uni didn’t really.

Interviewer:	OK so have you found the transition from education to work fairly easy then?

Subject:	Yeah except getting up every morning at the same time yeah.

Interviewer:	It's just a different routine it's like…

Subject:	It's a better routine actually because you just go to work and then you're finished, apart from I’ve got my dissertation to do, but that’s detail, but yeah it's just like 9 to 5 and then that's it you don’t have to you know go to lectures 9 to 5 and then work until 10 or 11 o’clock at night you know and that's quite nice. I like that bit.

Interviewer:	Do you think that it will be difficult when you go back to uni then?

Subject:	No I think erm I will have changed quite a bit and you know you learn what you need to do, what's important, you prioritise differently and I think I’ll be all right. I think I’ll just go to lectures and if I haven’t got anything in between I’ll do some work you know. Like before you just sit about and chat or doss about, I think I've got better now and I think because most of my year group are on industry this year. I think it's the same for them as well, so it will be all right.

Interviewer:	OK have you had to face any new issues at work like office politics and stuff like that?

Subject:	I don’t know what you mean.

Interviewer:	Or dealing with different people instead of just students I suppose, like with the clients and has that been easy or difficult?

Subject:	I haven’t had a problem erm I mean you have, you have to chat to people to understand what's going on like it's quite hard to chat to some of the operators because they have been there for you know some of them have been there 30, 40 years and you come up with a new idea and they're like a bit – but you have to chat to them to get them on side and then you get feedback from them and you need to understand how it works, like really how it works you know I mean obviously with you might understand it from an engineering point of view but an operator needs to, you know, it needs to be easy for them to operate and…so I mean it's just (inaudible) but I mean I think I've been all right with that actually.

Interviewer:	OK do you think that educational experience reflects what it's like in industry at all?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	Or should it?

Subject:	I don’t see how it can. I mean all you can do you know in a lecture hall is you know learn the basics, all the (inaudible) you know and just try and appreciate what, what goes on but you until you actually see it you know you can't learn from them. Even in the lab you try and I mean the lab is slightly closer to industry but it's tiny, it's just, it's just so small you just don’t appreciate like how big things are and how complex things can be, until you see it really.

Interviewer:	OK, so would you say that university and work have different in priorities and goals?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	What...

Subject:	Well a company wants to make money and uni just wants to you know, take your money. You know they provide your education but you don’t have to be there.

Interviewer:	OK how many women do [company] employ?

Subject:	How do you mean employ? I mean obviously there's like me and my boss we’re the only female engineers, then there's erm...

Interviewer:	Out of how many? Is that out of a lot?

Subject:	I work, in the engineering department there's only about … 15 or 20 and then there's obviously the receptionist is female and HR are female and some of the accountants are female. The cleaners are all female and then there's some chemists as well.

Interviewer:	Operators and stuff like that?

Subject:	There's no operators that are female at all.

Interviewer:	OK does [company] have a programme or structure that's in place for placement students to follow while you're there?

Subject:	Not really I mean we’re, we just do the same work as everyone else. Like I say I work in the engineering department...

Interviewer:	Yes (inaudible).

Subject:	Sorry?

Interviewer:	So you don’t feel that you’ve been treated like a student? 

Subject:	No I mean obviously initially you know you work up to it I mean now I'm getting like real projects where I can spend some money and stuff that's nice but it's just the same. I mean the problem - there’ll be a problem on the plant or there's been a problem there for years and or they’ll just want to put some new equipment in to make more money and so in the engineering department you’ll get given this project and you’ll get a team and sometimes I’ll be in that team and sometimes there’ll be different projects that I won't be in. So you need to get 3 or 4 people at the minimum in a, that are engineers in a team and all their different experiences ands it's just the same I mean obviously when you first start you're input in the project isn’t as much I mean you’ll just be doing simple things like flow sheets erm like working procedures that kind of thing. I would say more of the boring stuff really erm and then you gradually I mean like I'm, I'm like appointed project engineer for 2 projects now so I’m like the top one kind of thing as it were.

Interviewer:	So it's actually building experience?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	OK does the company say what they hope for you to achieve as a placement student? Do they have goals set for you or anything like that?

Subject:	Not really I think you just go along and do your do your projects and stuff.

Interviewer:	Yeah and you're happy with how that's going then?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you think it would be a good idea to have some structure in place or because your placement seems to be going quite well anyway, it probably doesn’t matter?

Subject:	Well I mean I don’t I mean I suppose you can have structure in that you have to do a project on certain different areas. I think that just happens anyway erm and I don’t really see how you could have a very like a rigid structure because it I mean you know one year like the year I've got, loads of work has been done over the last couple of years and now we’re just kind of installing it. So I'm doing more of like a commissioning thing which is you're putting it in and when you’ve finished installing it erm whereas I know the student last year she didn’t do any commissioning at all. And, then she did a lot more of the actual like raw design and started off with like nothing and was given this idea and did the thing but I'm like a step further on with my project.

Interviewer:	It's just the stage the company is at?

Subject:	Yeah so I don’t really see how that could be all that rigid.

Interviewer:	OK is your job or your role in the company what you expected it to be then?

Subject:	I didn’t really have any expectations to be honest. I didn’t really know what I was going to be doing or. I just heard that it was a good placement from the last year’s student and the student before and the one before probably.

Interviewer:	Are they all at Loughborough?

Subject:	Yeah, yeah so they’ve only had Loughborough students for the last few years.

Interviewer:	OK, do you feel like you have been given an appropriate level of responsibility then?

Subject:	Yeah, yeah definitely erm it's just they’ve got to know that you're competent to do it as well and that yeah now I've definitely been given that.

Interviewer:	Do you feel like the company are quite supportive of you as either as a new recruit or placement student?

Subject:	The company as a whole?

Interviewer:	Yeah.

Subject:	Erm hmm I don’t – sometimes. Sometimes, they're you know not very helpful at all.

Interviewer:	In what sort of way?

Subject:	Well because on one in one aspect I'm employed by the company full time but then I'm just a part time employee as well because I've got a limited contract. So obviously there are certain things that you don’t, benefits, most benefits you don’t get at all which is fair enough like pension you know that's obvious really I think. But, they're a bit erm you know I mean like with sick pay I don’t get sick pay at all, which is a little bit annoying because I've been ill like I've been to the doctors and I've got medication that kind of thing and can prove that I've been to the doctors. It's not like I've been skiving or hung over and so they just dock my wages for that for example. But I know last years placement student got, was it sick pay?

Interviewer:	Well that's interesting.

Subject:	So yeah I've been trying to find her contract because I think they're exactly the same so er...

Interviewer:	OK have you spoken to the university about things like that at all then?

Subject:	What can they do? I don’t think they can do anything I mean all I can do is try and get last year’s placement student’s contract but she can't find it so.

Interviewer:	Yeah okay what about within sort of your team? Are they supportive of you?

Subject:	Yeah, yeah definitely.

Interviewer:	And you're happy to speak to them if you’ve got problems or if you wanted more or less responsibility?

Subject:	Erm yes I mean it's all right I mean I chat to my boss quite a lot she’s really, really helpful and then all the engineers have different you know they’re all different engineers. So, it's just a matter of learning which is the right one to talk to for a particular problem or I mean I haven’t – I’d say I’ve only really really, spoke to probably half properly, you know, needed their help. I mean everyone else I've chatted to over minor issues but only about half of them I've had proper, proper contact with.

Interviewer:	So is most of the work that you're doing in team work?

Subject:	Yeah all of it.

Interviewer:	OK, how do you think that compares to doing team work at uni?

Subject:	Erm, I'd say it's easier at work. Because not everyone is coming in as an engineer. So, you’ve got erm you’ve just got different engineers, which obviously have different education and they’ve all been at work for years, and years and years as well so they just have a different look on a problem and initially it's good because you’ve got loads and loads of ideas erm whereas with chemical engineers obviously you do have loads of ideas but it's all the same. You know, so I mean it is, it's better at work and if someone wants to, you know, achieve that goal I mean if you're in a team at uni the chances are that some people aren’t bothered at all erm, I think they're probably different a lot different next year. Chatting to a lot of my mates that are on industry about it, but so far they're yeah I mean if people don’t want to do the work they're not going to do it so.

Interviewer:	Do you think because you're all different types of engineers at work as well you all have more of a specific role within a team?

Subject:	Yeah, yes.

Interviewer:	Which makes things easier?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you think then that if team work at uni is totally different it is worth while doing it at uni still?

Subject:	Erm what when I come back next year?

Interviewer:	Or the team work you’ve done all ready?

Subject:	Oh I’d say yeah I mean it's very useful buts it's completely for a different reason? (OK) Erm, obviously in a team you're going to get leaders and you're going to get people that are just going to you know want to be told what to do. Erm and team work up to your placement year erm definitely erm you know tries to I mean not doesn’t want to make everyone a leader but wants for everyone to contribute and I think that you know, after 2 years of doing that at uni it definitely achieves it towards the end you know most people are you know willing to contribute and willing to do the work. Obviously there are exceptions to that but initially when you do it you obviously get natural leaders and natural just you know sit in the corner people. So I definitely it helps yes just to bring people out of their selves it's just a confidence thing I think.

Interviewer:	Yeah, so even though they are different, you are still gaining skills when you do it?

Subject:	Yeah but just I'm not, I would just say people skills not erm any type of education skills.

Interviewer:	OK that's fine, how would you summarise the placement experience so far then?

Subject:	Erm, hmm I just love it, it's challenging definitely and it does teach you a lot.

Interviewer:	So it's been a positive experience?

Subject:	Oh yeah definitely, definitely (inaudible).

Interviewer:	What has been the best and the worst things about it?

Subject:	Erm, the best thing is like finishing, finishing projects. Erm, I mean when I first got there they were, I’ve just been on this project and they’d just finished about a couple of weeks ago and we had to – part of the plant was used for I don’t know 20 or 30 years and they put it out – they shut it down. And it's it just makes erm hard water and soft water basically and er when we finished it and we spent, I don’t know, 50 grand on it but we finished it a couple of weeks ago and that's cool, that's nice. The worst bit is probably at the beginning it was boring but it's got to be, there has got to be a learning curve hasn’t there? You’ve just got to, I mean don’t think it would be any, yeah I thought it was boring. I was just learning where everything was and what goes on and you know the boring bits. (Yeah) And the worst thing as well is getting up in the morning because sometimes I start early and sometimes I start at 7. (Cor blimey!) so I have to leave home at half six and get up at 6 and I hate that, absolutely hate that.

Interviewer:	Yeah I don’t blame you. Is there anything that you thought that you would achieve but haven’t so far?

Subject:	I didn’t really like I said I didn’t have any expectations. I mean I want to do some more design work but I'm getting that now so and I spoke to my boss a few weeks ago about that and I'm getting the work now, so. 

Interviewer:	Yeah okay, do you think that you’ve changed personally as a result of doing the placement?

Subject:	Erm, just prioritise differently now. Erm you just kind of appreciate you know just appreciate different things differently and erm I don’t know I miss being a student obviously. But yeah I am different just different responsibilities you know you’ve got, you can't go out every night, you’ve got to get up in the morning and go to work. You just have to do that that's the way it is. That's what you know most of the country do isn’t it and that's what I'm going to be doing in a year or so.

Interviewer:	So do you think it's helped prepare you for when you start work for real?

Subject:	Yeah, yeah, yeah well I don’t think it, I wouldn’t say it's a shock starting work. Because I knew I was only going to be here a year. But if I had just done my degree and then started work I would have probably been like, for the first couple of months just you know really taken aback by… (Yeah) But working is great because people don’t anything on a Friday afternoon or a Monday morning. In fact it's like a 3 day week really.

Interviewer:	Just you wouldn’t mind Monday and Fridays off?

Subject:	Yeah Mondays are just like you know winding up for the week and Fridays are definitely winding down for the week.

Interviewer:	Okay do you think you’ll use what you're learning now in your final year?

Subject:	Erm I don’t know I've looked at modules and I don’t plan to use that much apart from design. (Yeah) Erm I've got I think I've got 2 design modules, there's an individual one and a team one and erm we've done design projects before but now obviously you really appreciate that there’ll be several answers to a problem but you’ve got to look at the cost and safety as well. Which I wouldn’t have done before so that will be good that will useful in those modules. I've got something to do with pollution control and I think that will be well what I’ve done so far will be very helpful with that but I don’t think anything else will be all that not, not, not…

Interviewer:	Not specific?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you just think it will be more general things like how you work in a team and things like that, that you mentioned earlier then?

Subject:	That will?

Interviewer:	That will help you or how you work rather than the actual …

Subject:	Just the way you approach a problem really erm you just you have there's just so many more things to consider in the team work thing. When you’ve got a problem and yeah working in a team will definitely be a lot different now but better. (Yeah) A lot better.

Interviewer:	Okay I take it that there aren’t any other placement students at the organisation?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	Do you think it would be good if there were or?

Subject:	Erm, not really in my department I wouldn’t have thought unless they were a different type of engineer because it's it is quite a small company but then they could be…they could have a chemist which I wouldn’t really be in contact with ever well probably once a month kind of thing. But, not another chemical engineer there isn’t enough I mean my boss is a chemical engineer as well so, you know there isn’t really enough erm.

Interviewer:	Have you been in contact with students at uni then still that are on placement?

Subject:	Hmm, yeah.

Interviewer:	Have you kind of supported each other?

Subject:	Yeah definitely I mean there's a few of us and we’re like I say I mean we don’t e-mail everyday or whatever but if there's problems then you know we’ll have a bit of a chat on the internet as it were and it's good actually. I mean I had a problem a few weeks ago with thermal expansion in a pipe of a fluid, and just I had got loads of ideas and we don’t really use any of those ideas at work. So, everything that I thought would be a new idea and erm yeah it was really good getting their feedback really because obviously they use – they’ve got the answers at work yeah so – they kind of can see it more and tell me things about it you know really help me out with it – so that was good.

Interviewer:	Okay, do you feel that you're treated as a permanent member of staff, you know you said not by the organisation as a whole, but within your team?

Subject:	Erm, yes and no I mean a lot of the work – like I said before, the company is you know, not making any money and I don’t think it’s going to be around for many, many more years. So everyone does look short term anyway. Erm I'd say hmm it depends. Sometimes I mean if I'm properly involved in a project then I think I do get looked on as a full time, you know, engineer, but in the bigger picture I'm just you know just there for a little bit and I finish, you know, finish in the summer. There's not really that long left is it so I'm not, I’m not counting down to it yet, but I will be definitely will be, just to getting back to being a student.

Interviewer:	Yeah looking forward to getting back?

Subject:	Oh yeah yes definitely.

Interviewer:	Okay, going back to the teamwork thing, has there been anyone that you’ve particularly liked or disliked working with?

Subject:	You're always going to get that aren’t you? Erm, yeah some of the blokes are a bit you know particularly some of the old blokes like I said some of the operators and actually some of the engineers because I'm young and I'm female they're a bit and obviously a student which I don’t think helps at all. I have to, well not so much any more but at the beginning like if I had an idea or an opinion or whatever I definitely had to really, really back it up and you know properly, you know, say what I'm thinking and what's going on. Whereas now it's just like, oh yeah and you just mention it and then you have a discussion about it whereas before it was definitely me talking and saying my thing and then it would be just brushed under the carpet a lot of the time. Which is fair enough because I didn’t really like have any idea about environmental stuff or cost or anything but…

Interviewer:	Do you think that that's just because they're not used to …

Subject:	Well there's been students there for years erm so I don’t know.

Interviewer:	And female students as well …

Subject:	Yeah but I mean the student last year I don’t think she was, nothing, she’s nothing like me at all for starters, which is fair enough. It would be getting a bit weird if there was 2 of me, but I don’t think she was so like, like I think I've I think I'm quite involved in what I do you know. I want to, you know, I want to achieve this goal as quickly as I can really, may as well get it done hadn’t you? Erm, and I yeah I just think they're probably just not used to me but that's fair enough.

Interviewer:	You accepted how they were then?

Subject:	Sorry?

Interviewer:	You accepted that's just the way people are then?

Subject:	Yeah, you’ve got to haven’t you, there's nothing I can do about it.

Interviewer:	Do you think that sort of experience will help prepare you for when you start work? That people…

Subject:	Yeah definitely, definitely everybody’s different aren’t they?

Interviewer:	Were you surprised that people had that attitude or is it what you were expecting?

Subject:	No, I wasn’t expecting it but I suppose I was because people are like that aren’t they? Everywhere, so I wouldn’t say I was really expecting it but it's just the way it is.

Interviewer:	Ok have you been give a mentor at all in the company?

Subject:	Not really, there's my boss and we chat a lot and we have like some work reviews yeah I've only had two of them though because I don’t really need them but I chat to her on a day-to-day basis and you know it's not always about work sometimes it's you know just like a chat really and I suppose in a way she is my mentor but …

Interviewer:	Is she the person that you go to if you need advice or anything and stuff like that then?

Subject:	Depends on the problem but yeah most of the time.

Interviewer:	Okay, would you have liked to have been given a mentor in a more official way or anything?

Subject:	No I think if you don’t have that then it's to pay you more for work if you have a mentor it's like a tutor at uni isn’t it? (Yeah) And er yeah it's better just the way it is, I like it the way it is.

Interviewer:	Okay do you feel anyone at work has ever given you any bad advice or?

Subject:	Yeah more than likely, yeah. I mean you know you ask someone a question because you’ve got a problem or whatever and sometimes they're just, they’ll say it from experience, you know. Well, for years and years and years we've done this – whereas this might be the wrong way because, you know, it's dangerous or, you know. So, it's I don’t think they mean to give the bad advice but it's just yeah I mean like I said before, health & safety and environmental rules are changing all of the time, erm and I suppose they're just not aware really. If it's not their field then it would just be something that they’ve done all the time and you know – why not keep doing it so…

Interviewer:	OK is there anyone in the company that you regard as like a role model?

Subject:	No, no.

Interviewer:	OK has anyone from uni been to visit you on placement yet?

Subject:	Yeah erm someone from the department came over he was here for about half an hour and drank coffee for 20 minutes of that so it was a bit pointless really.

Interviewer:	Did they explain why they were coming to visit you?

Subject:	Well, they just have to, we still pay tuition fees and you know we've got to pay quite a lot for that visit I feel.

Interviewer:	So it's not really worthwhile then?

Subject:	No well if they're coming to visit then they have to visit properly. Because his visit, I was the third student of three that he visited that day and he just wasn’t bothered when came for me. It was, there was just no point in him being there. You know he had his couple of questions on a bit of paper that he had scribbled down you know while I was getting his coffee kind of thing erm and it was I don’t know it was just pointless in him being there, absolutely pointless. I mean we have to, you know, kind of report, put a report in each month to you know my industrial tutor and somebody else in the department.

Interviewer:	And what sorts of things do you have to put on?

Subject:	You just put on what projects you’ve been doing that's all I write I don’t know what you're supposed to write really. You see I don’t know what I'm supposed to write.

Interviewer:	So the university haven’t been very supportive in that sense?

Subject:	You just write a report and they’re due in on the 10th of each month and …

Interviewer:	But you're not really told what the purpose of the report is?

Subject:	Not really I mean I'm just going on what the placement student last year did which is just write about the projects and that's what I've been doing and saying what I'm doing. But no I thought it was pretty pointless in him coming and I don’t think he’ll come again. He should do he’s supposed to come twice but I don’t think he will.

Interviewer:	Did you know the person that came to visit you?

Subject:	He's lectured me yeah, he didn’t really know who I am but that's fair enough I like it that way so.

Interviewer:	OK did they speak to your boss?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	No?

Subject:	No. They spoke to my boss’s boss but not about me.

Interviewer:	Right.

Subject:	They just had a bit of a chat.

Interviewer:	So it just seemed like a total waste of time?

Subject:	Oh yes he came and he asked about my dissertation but he came in October so I hadn’t started it. I had done a little bit of research but it's not due until next October well October/ November this year so you know I'm not going to have started it by then and that's all he talked about really. Told me how to use the library too - I thought that was really helpful, I’ve never been to the library yet (sarcastic).

Interviewer:	So would you be happy to go to that person if you had a problem at all?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	Is there anyone in university that you'd go to if you had a problem?

Subject:	I'd speak to my tutor my personal tutor from, I don’t really see my personal tutor anymore but I'd speak to him. (Yeah) But I don’t know, I mean, you see problems at work I'd….

Interviewer:	You'd rather sort out …

Subject:	Well I'd sort out at work yeah they're separate aren’t they?

Interviewer:	Yeah okay do you know if either university or [company] have a complaints procedure if anything should go wrong?
